_what: Asymptotic cost of every estimator family, derived from the code and checked against measurement. Numbers only -- no manuscript prose was edited.

protocol.load_note: Three other claude processes were resident. Every figure below is a back-to-back median inside ONE process on the same n grid, so RATIOS and LOG-LOG SLOPES are sound. Absolute milliseconds are advisory and should be re-taken on a quiet box before they are quoted as absolutes.
protocol.statistic: median of 2-5 repeats after warm-up (JIT and first call outside the clock)
protocol.geometry: uniform on [0,1000]^d unless noted; greedy crossover also checked on 20-cluster Gaussian
protocol.cross_check: compute_features(d=2, n=85900) measured here at 1312 ms against the published harness GART 2.0 feature_time of 1365 ms on pla85900 -- 3.9% apart, so this bench reproduces the published protocol.

derived_complexity._reading: n points, d dimensions. 'dominant' is the leading term as implemented, not as the algorithm is usually quoted.

classical_closed_forms.dominant_term_source: np.unique(coords, axis=0) row-dedup in the shared estimate() wrapper -- a void-view lexsort, O(d n log n). The published arithmetic is O(nd) and is a rounding error next to it.

hull_variant.branch: region_from_points(prefer_hull=True) calls ConvexHull only when d <= HULL_MAX_DIM = 3
hull_variant.d_le_3: O(n log n), Qhull; measured 5.9 ms at n=85900 d=2, 17% of BHH total, log-log slope 0.674 (SUBlinear -- hull vertex count grows like log n for uniform points, so per-point cost falls)
hull_variant.d_ge_4: hull is never computed; silently falls through to the O(nd) bounding box and records region_source='bounding_box'
hull_variant.consequence: the exponential n^floor(d/2) hull blow-up the paper cites as a motivation is switched off by the cap and never occurs at runtime. Verified: BHH at d=50 n=1000 returns region_source='bounding_box'.

classical_closed_forms.sampling_region_variant: O(nd); region_from_grid is O(1) and no hull or bbox pass runs on the region itself

branch_1_delaunay.condition: d <= 3 and n >= d+2 (tried FIRST, at every n)
branch_1_delaunay.cost: O(n log n) time, O(n) memory
branch_1_delaunay.constant_dominated_by: Qhull Delaunay, then np.unique on ~3n (d=2) or ~6n (d=3) candidate edge rows, then scipy Kruskal on the sparse graph
branch_1_delaunay.d3_penalty: d=3 costs 6.2x d=3-vs-d=2 at n=10000 (307.9 ms vs 49.9 ms) -- more tetrahedra per point and 6 edges each

branch_2_dense.condition: d >= 4 and 16*n^2 bytes <= MST_DENSE_BUDGET_GB (default 8 GiB) => n <= 23170
branch_2_dense.cost: O(n^2 d) for cdist + O(n^2 log n) for scipy's Kruskal over the ~n^2 materialized edges; the SORT dominates for d < log n
branch_2_dense.memory: peak ~12 n^2 bytes (float64 cdist then float32 cast) plus scipy's CSR buffers

branch_3_blocked_prim.condition: n > 23170 with d >= 4, or Delaunay raises
branch_3_blocked_prim.cost: Theta(n^2 d) time, O(n) memory, numba scalar loop, no sort

switch_points: n = 23170 at d >= 4 (dense to blocked Prim), memory-driven not time-driven
mst_ratio_family.discrepancy: The manuscript's O(n^2 d) row is wrong on both benchmarks where these models are timed. In d<=3 the code takes Delaunay and is O(n log n); in d>=4 the implemented dominant term is the n^2 log n Kruskal sort, not n^2 d.

gart2.total: Theta(n log n) in d<=3; Theta(n^2 d + n^2 log n) in d>=4 -- i.e. exactly the MST family's class, times a constant

pca_canonicalize.note: 0.2% of the block at d=2; only competitive with the MST when d^2 approaches n

tree_diameter.note: slope exceeds 1 because it is a pure-Python deque BFS over a list-of-lists adjacency -- pointer chasing, so the constant grows with working-set size

dense_branch.cost: Theta(n^2 d) time, Theta(n^2) memory (cdist, 8n^2 bytes)

candlist_branch.cost: O(n log n) worst case; Theta(n) as measured
candlist_branch.why_not_n_log_n: The kd-tree work (build + one batched k=17 query, C code) is O(n log n) but only 31-35% of the pass. The other 65-69% is the main loop: n-1 iterations of ~6 NumPy calls each, at a FLAT 3.44-3.64 us/step across n=10k..86k. An interpreted Theta(n) term with a microsecond constant swamps the log factor over every n the paper reports.
candlist_branch.rebuild_policy: tree rebuilt when stale >= 0.5*|remaining|, so rebuild cost telescopes geometrically to O(n log n) amortized

inference.cost: O(K * Dbar) = O(1) in n and d
inference.constant_dominated_by: pandas DataFrame construction and the LightGBM Python predict() wrapper, NOT tree traversal. Evidence: LGBM_V3 has fewer trees yet infers in 3.872 ms, 3.0x slower than GART 2.0's 1118-tree ensemble.

gart1.cost: Theta(n^2 d) time AND Theta(n^2) memory
gart1.dominant_term_source: cdist(coords, coords) materialized purely to take a per-row min for the 1-NN mean/std. Two scalars bought with an n x n matrix.
gart1.hard_failure: no pla85900 row exists in the timing corpus for GART 1.0; the dense matrix at n=85900 needs ~59 GB. GART 2.0 completes the same instance in 1.399 s.
gart1.unguarded_hull: _calculate_gart_features calls ConvexHull with no dimension cap (unlike classical_region_estimators' HULL_MAX_DIM=3), so it would hit the n^floor(d/2) blow-up at d>=4. Moot in practice -- GART 1.0 is only ever run at d=2.

hilbert.as_implemented: Theta(n d p) interpreted + O(n log n) argsort, with the FIRST term dominating
hilbert.dominant_term_source: HilbertCurve.distances_from_points over a Python list-of-lists -- pure-Python bit interleaving, n*d*p operations at interpreter speed. The argsort is invisible next to it.
hilbert.note: the only estimator measured whose per-point cost does not drift at all; O(n log n) is a correct upper bound but Theta(n d p) is what the machine executes

learned_controls.linear_31f_and_nn_31f: identical feature block to GART 2.0, so identical Theta(n log n) / Theta(n^2 d) feature cost; the head is O(1) in n
learned_controls.nn_head: 4 gated residual blocks at hidden_dim 192 => ~1.5e5 FLOPs per prediction, O(1) in n; measured 1.534 ms, again wrapper-dominated
learned_controls.lgbm_v3_and_nn_v3_are_cheaper_at_large_n: 0.889 s and 0.883 s against GART 2.0's 1.399 s at pla85900, because the V3 30-feature set omits greedy_nn_over_mst. The 0.510 s gap is that one feature (measured standalone at 0.450 s).

held_karp_1tree_bound.STATUS: NOT IMPLEMENTED ANYWHERE IN THE REPOSITORY
held_karp_1tree_bound.searched: *.py, *.tex, *.md -- the only 'Held-Karp' in the codebase is solvers/exact.py's exponential bitmask DP, which is the exact solver and is explicitly flagged in tsp_utils_2 as 'misnamed historically'. No Lagrangian ascent, no subgradient loop, no 1-tree anywhere.
held_karp_1tree_bound.consequence: the manuscript's middle-ground claim currently has no measured upper anchor
held_karp_1tree_bound.derived_cost_per_ascent_iteration: Theta(n^2 d) -- a minimum spanning tree on V\{1} under the perturbed cost c'_ij = c_ij + pi_i + pi_j, plus an O(n) scan for the two cheapest edges at node 1
held_karp_1tree_bound.why_no_delaunay_fast_path: The node potentials pi break the Euclidean metric, so after iteration 1 the perturbed MST is NOT a subgraph of the Delaunay triangulation. The O(n log n) route that MST_Only and GART 2.0 both take in d<=3 is unavailable to the 1-tree bound at every iteration but the first. This is the structural reason the bound is a whole complexity class above the MST family rather than a constant factor above it.
held_karp_1tree_bound.total: Theta(k n^2 d) for k ascent iterations

measured_fair_implementation.note: numba O(n^2) Prim reading perturbed cost on the fly, O(n) memory -- deliberately efficient so the anchor is not a strawman

measured_naive_scipy_implementation.note: dense perturbed matrix + scipy minimum_spanning_tree (Kruskal, n^2 sort) -- reported so the anchor's sensitivity to implementation is visible

exact_solver.bitmask_dp: Theta(n^2 2^n) time, Theta(n 2^n) memory; at n=20 the dp array alone is 8*20*2^20 = 168 MB
exact_solver.concorde: branch-and-cut; no polynomial bound, worst case exponential

middle_ground_ledger_d2._what: the claim the paper needs, with both sides measured. n=1000 and n=16000, d=2.
middle_ground_ledger_d2.interpretation: GART 2.0 holds a FLAT 2.0-2.3x over the MST-ratio family across four orders of magnitude in n -- same complexity class, constant multiplier. Against the 1-tree bound the gap GROWS as Theta(n/log n), from 7.7x at n=1000 to 211x at n=16000, because the 1-tree is Theta(k n^2) with no Delaunay path and GART 2.0 is Theta(n log n). The 6.05x penalty against Hilbert at n<100 is fixed inference overhead, not scaling; it decays to 2.14x by n>10000.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: brief states the greedy-NN pass 'adds roughly 95 ms at n>10,000'
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: 95 ms is a point value at n~20000 that has been read as a plateau. The pass is Theta(n) and unbounded; at pla85900 it is 4.7x the quoted figure and 34% of the entire feature block.
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.constant_hiding_what: nothing algorithmic. 65-69% of the pass is the interpreted main loop at a flat 3.4-3.6 us/step; the kd-tree O(n log n) C work is the minority. The derived complexity is right; the growth is linear and the constant is the Python interpreter.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: mst_utils.compute_mst prefers _dense_mst for d>=4 up to n=23170, on the stated rationale that 'dense wins up to its memory limit'
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: _blocked_prim_mst beats _dense_mst by 42-123x on every (n,d) pair tested. n=1000 d=4: 122.5 ms vs 1.7 ms (70.6x). n=4000 d=4: 2674 ms vs 21.8 ms (122.8x). The gap WIDENS with n.
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: The rationale compares dense against Delaunay, which is sound, but the dispatch then applies it against blocked Prim, which it never tested. Dense pays an n^2 log n Kruskal sort over ~n^2 materialized edges; Prim pays n^2 d with no sort and O(n) memory. Prim dominates on both axes.
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.blast_radius: every d>=4 instance below n=23170 -- i.e. the entire 16,920-instance ND benchmark (n<=1000, d up to 100). Not a correctness issue and it does not touch the published TSPLIB timing column, which is all d=2 Delaunay. It does mean any ND wall-clock number is inflated ~40-120x, and it makes the ND benchmark far more expensive to regenerate than it needs to be.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: feature_engineering_gart2.DENSE_CAP = 3000, documented as 'n at or below which the dense (JIT) greedy path is cheaper than building k-NN candidate lists'
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: crossover is n ~ 2100 on uniform points and n ~ 2200 on 20-cluster Gaussian points. At the cap itself, dense costs 30.0 ms against candlist's 19.0 ms.
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: the cap is ~1.4x too high; instances in 2100 < n <= 3000 pay up to 58% more than necessary on the greedy pass. Robust across both geometries tested, so it is not a clustering artifact.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: manuscript Table (benchmark models) lists the classical closed forms at O(nd)
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: np.unique(coords, axis=0) inside the shared estimate() wrapper is 29% of BHH's runtime at n=1000 rising to 79% at n=85900
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: as implemented they are Theta(d n log n), not O(nd). The published arithmetic really is O(nd); the wrapper's row-dedup is what the clock sees. Either state the wrapper cost or note that the O(nd) figure excludes preprocessing shared by all models.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: manuscript Table lists MST_Only / Asymptotic / Calibrated rho(d) / Calibrated rho(d,n) / Linear / NN at O(n^2 d)
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: all of them route through compute_mst, which takes the Delaunay branch at d<=3 -- measured slope 1.145, 633 ms at n=85900, not quadratic
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: the O(n^2 d) row is wrong for the 2D and TSPLIB benchmarks, which are exactly where these models are timed. Line 219 already grants the O(n log n) Delaunay path to GART 2.0; the same path is taken by every one of these rows. In d>=4 the row is also mis-stated, since the implemented dominant term is n^2 log n (Kruskal) rather than n^2 d.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: manuscript line 219: 'Below n=3000 the greedy tour, not the MST, is therefore the leading term of 2D extraction'
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: n=500: MST 2.57 ms vs greedy 0.80 ms (MST leads). n=1000: 4.65 vs 3.54 (MST leads). n=2000: 9.04 vs 13.60 (greedy leads). n=3000: 13.89 vs 29.96 (greedy leads).
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: true only on roughly 1500 <= n <= 3000, not for all n below 3000. Below n~1500 the MST is still the leading term.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: manuscript line 283 lists the Hilbert baseline at O(n log n)
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: slope 0.990 with r^2 0.999 and per-point cost flat at 6.2-6.4 us across n=51..85900
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: correct as an upper bound but not what dominates. The executed cost is Theta(n d p) in interpreted Python (p=16 bit-interleaving over a list-of-lists); the argsort's log factor is not detectable.

discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.claim: convex-hull cost 'matters and differs by d'
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.measured: d=2 hull is 5.9 ms at n=85900 -- 0.4% of GART 2.0, 17% of BHH -- with a SUBlinear slope of 0.674. For d>=4 HULL_MAX_DIM=3 switches the hull off entirely.
discrepancies_theory_vs_measurement.verdict: the hull never costs anything at runtime in this codebase. The n^floor(d/2) blow-up cited in the introduction as motivation is real in theory but is disabled by the cap, so it should be presented as a design reason for the cap rather than as a measured cost of the classical baselines.

measured_slopes_n_ge_3000._what: log-log exponent p in t ~ n^p
